questions.prompt: The ISP has delegated a /48, but the downstream interface has no IPv6 prefix. What is the first configuration relationship to verify?

options.text: Add a static route for the ISP /48 and enable DHCPv4 relay.
options.feedback: A route does not create the delegated prefix or bind the IA_PD to the downstream interface.

options.text: Match the downstream delegated-prefix IAID and upstream-interface reference to the received IA_PD.
options.feedback: The IAID binds the upstream lease to the downstream interface; a mismatch leaves the child interface unnumbered.

options.text: Change the prefix hint to /64 and restart the DHCPv6 server.
options.feedback: The hint is a preference to the provider, not the installed prefix or IAID mapping.

options.text: Enable NAT66 on the downstream interface and renew the client lease.
options.feedback: NAT66 does not repair DHCPv6-PD acquisition or the IAID relationship.

questions.prompt: The provider returns a different prefix than the configured ::/48 hint. What should the engineer conclude?

options.text: The hint is a request preference; use the actual delegated prefix and its lifetimes.
options.feedback: The provider controls the allocation. Downstream interfaces must follow the installed IA_PD, not the requested hint.

options.text: The ISP has violated DHCPv6 because the hint must be returned exactly.
options.feedback: Prefix hints are not guarantees; the server can delegate another suitable prefix.

options.text: The FortiGate has silently converted the /48 into a DHCPv6 relay.
options.feedback: Prefix delegation is a lease relationship, not a relay conversion.

options.text: The downstream interface must be assigned the hint as a static address.
options.feedback: A static prefix can become stale when the provider renews or changes the delegation.

questions.prompt: The core FortiGate has a valid IA_PD, but LAN clients receive no IPv6 configuration. Which path should be checked next?

options.text: Increase the ISP prefix hint length and clear the IPv6 routing table.
options.feedback: Changing the hint does not enable client addressing on the downstream segment.

options.text: Verify downstream Router Advertisements or DHCPv6 server operation and the matching delegated IAID.
options.feedback: The upstream lease can be valid while the downstream client-advertisement path is missing.

options.text: Enable DHCPv4 relay on the LAN and renew the IPv4 leases.
options.feedback: DHCPv4 relay does not distribute an IPv6 delegated prefix.

options.text: Replace the upstream IA_PD client with a static IPv6 address.
options.feedback: A static upstream address does not solve the missing downstream RA/DHCPv6 service.

questions.prompt: IPv6 addresses work on downstream clients, but DNS resolution fails after prefix delegation. Which setting is most directly relevant?

options.text: Change the downstream IAID to match the DNS server address.
options.feedback: IAID identifies the prefix association, not the DNS server.

options.text: Enable DHCPv4 option 6 on the delegated interface.
options.feedback: DHCPv4 option 6 does not supply DNS to IPv6-only clients.

options.text: Add a static route for the DNS server without checking resolver delivery.
options.feedback: Routing may be correct while clients have no DNS server configured.

options.text: Check delegated DNS propagation and the downstream DHCPv6 DNS service or RA RDNSS.
options.feedback: Address assignment and DNS delivery are separate; the clients must receive usable resolver information.

questions.prompt: A restricted administrator must use a protected address object in a policy but must not edit its definition. What is the expected behavior?

options.text: The administrator cannot see or reference the protected object anywhere.
options.feedback: FortiManager explicitly allows protected objects to be selected in policy packages.

options.text: The administrator can edit the object but cannot install the policy package.
options.feedback: Protection blocks editing, not the use of the object in a policy.

options.text: The administrator can modify the object only while workspace mode is enabled.
options.feedback: Workspace mode is separate from Protected Objects permission.

options.text: The administrator can reference the protected object, but its definition remains read-only.
options.feedback: FortiManager separates permission to consume an object from permission to modify its definition.

questions.prompt: The Protected toggle is missing for every administrator, including the object owner. What should be checked first?

options.text: Enable ADOM workspace mode and restart the managed FortiGates.
options.feedback: Workspace mode does not expose the Protected Objects feature.

options.text: Assign the FortiGate super_admin profile to every FortiManager user.
options.feedback: Device-side profiles do not control FortiManager object protection.

options.text: Enable gui-object-protect globally so the Protected Objects controls are exposed.
options.feedback: The global visibility switch must be enabled before the administrator-profile permission can expose the controls.

options.text: Reinstall the policy package to regenerate the Protected column.
options.feedback: The column is controlled by FortiManager global and profile settings.

questions.prompt: A user can see the Protected column but still edits an object that should be protected. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The item is not marked protected, or the user has the Protected Objects permission.
options.feedback: Protection requires both per-item state and a user profile without the permission to change it.

options.text: The FortiGate has not received the latest policy package installation.
options.feedback: The control is enforced in FortiManager's management plane, not on the device.

options.text: The user is in the wrong firewall policy sequence number.
options.feedback: Policy order does not grant or remove object-protection permission.

options.text: The ADOM database needs a full rebuild before protection is enforced.
options.feedback: A rebuild is not the documented prerequisite for per-object protection.

questions.prompt: Which test best proves that Protected Objects works as designed?

options.text: Confirm that a protected policy installs successfully on one FortiGate.
options.feedback: Installation proves consumption, but not that edits are denied.

options.text: Use an owner and consumer account to test edit denial and successful policy reference.
options.feedback: The two-persona test proves both sides of the feature: guarded definition and continued policy reuse.

options.text: Check that the consumer account can view the object name in search.
options.feedback: Visibility alone does not prove the object is read-only.

options.text: Verify that workspace mode is set to normal on the ADOM.
options.feedback: Workspace mode does not demonstrate Protected Objects enforcement.

questions.prompt: An IOC alert is generated by a historical rescan. Which marker distinguishes it from a real-time match?

options.text: The alert always contains a FortiGate policy UUID in the message.
options.feedback: A policy UUID is not the documented marker for rescan-originated alerts.

options.text: The IOC record is stored only in the FortiAnalyzer event database.
options.feedback: The tag is the key distinction, not a separate storage database.

options.text: The alert severity is automatically raised to Critical during rescan.
options.feedback: Rescan origin does not itself define the severity.

options.text: The rescanned log and resulting alert carry the Ioc_Rescan tag.
options.feedback: The tag identifies the historical rescan path; real-time matches continue without that tag.

questions.prompt: The Rescan Tasks table is empty even though real-time IOC alerts exist. Which scope should be checked?

options.text: Increase the FortiGate traffic-log retention and reboot the analyzer.
options.feedback: Retention does not enable the rescan policy or satisfy its license requirement.

options.text: Verify the IOC license, global rescan switch, current-ADOM switch, and selected log types.
options.feedback: Real-time IOC can work while historical rescan remains disabled or unlicensed at either scope.

options.text: Change the event-handler severity from High to Critical.
options.feedback: Severity settings do not create historical rescan tasks.

options.text: Disable TIDB updates so the rescan scheduler can start.
options.feedback: Rescan depends on current threat intelligence, not on stopping package updates.

questions.prompt: IOC alerts appear to be based on stale or demo threat data. What is the strongest verification?

options.text: Inspect the IOC license and TIDB version/load time using the documented sqllogd statistics.
options.feedback: A valid service license and current threat database are prerequisites for meaningful IOC results.

options.text: Compare the FortiGate firmware build with the FortiAnalyzer GUI theme version.
options.feedback: Those versions do not establish IOC license or TIDB freshness.

options.text: Increase rescan-max-runner to the maximum CPU count immediately.
options.feedback: Concurrency changes throughput, not threat database freshness or license state.

options.text: Delete the old IOC event handlers and recreate the default handlers.
options.feedback: Event handlers cannot correct a stale or demo TIDB package.

questions.prompt: A large historical rescan competes with interactive reports. Which control directly affects concurrent rescan work?

options.text: Increase the notification throttle to the maximum value.
options.feedback: Notification throttle affects alert frequency, not the number of rescan workers.

options.text: Extend the FortiGate log upload interval to one day.
options.feedback: Log upload cadence does not control historical rescan concurrency.

options.text: Tune rescan-max-runner while considering CPU and database I/O contention.
options.feedback: The setting controls concurrent rescan workers; more workers can shorten backlog but increase resource contention.

options.text: Disable the current ADOM and let global settings process every log.
options.feedback: ADOM scope is required for selecting eligible logs and date ranges.

questions.prompt: Which OpenSSH security-key algorithms are explicitly supported by FortiSwitchOS 8.0.0?

options.text: sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256 and sk-ssh-ed25519 are the documented security-key algorithms.
options.feedback: The 8.0.0 release notes name these two FIDO2-backed OpenSSH security-key types.

options.text: ssh-rsa and ssh-dss are the documented FIDO2 security-key algorithms.
options.feedback: Those are legacy key algorithms, not the two supported security-key types named in the release notes.

options.text: ecdsa-sha2-nistp256 and ssh-ed25519 without security-key markers.
options.feedback: Ordinary keys are not the same as the documented sk-prefixed security-key algorithms.

options.text: x509-client-cert and eap-tls are the supported SSH security-key types.
options.feedback: Those are certificate/EAP terms, not OpenSSH security-key algorithms.

questions.prompt: An administrator uses a normal registered SSH public key that skips the password prompt. What security claim is safe?

options.text: It proves that every SSH login requires a hardware authenticator touch.
options.feedback: The normal public-key field does not prove a FIDO2 challenge occurred.

options.text: It proves that the administrator profile has full super-user privileges.
options.feedback: Authentication does not determine the command authorization profile.

options.text: It proves public-key authentication, not necessarily FIDO2-backed multi-factor authentication.
options.feedback: A static authorized key can authenticate without a password; that alone does not prove hardware-backed MFA.

options.text: It proves that the FortiSwitch has validated a RADIUS accounting record.
options.feedback: SSH public-key authentication is unrelated to RADIUS accounting.

questions.prompt: SSH authentication succeeds, but the administrator cannot run a configuration command. Which layer should be checked?

options.text: Regenerate the FIDO2 private key because the command was denied.
options.feedback: A command authorization denial occurs after authentication and is not fixed by regenerating the key.

options.text: Change the FortiSwitch management VLAN to match the user group.
options.feedback: VLAN placement does not grant administrator command permissions.

options.text: Inspect the administrator access profile and command permissions after key authentication.
options.feedback: Successful key exchange proves authentication; the admin profile controls what the account can do.

options.text: Disable trusted-host restrictions for all administrator accounts.
options.feedback: A successful login already passed the trusted-host check.

questions.prompt: A FIDO2 key is rejected before the administrator session starts. What is the best first comparison?

options.text: Change the switch spanning-tree root priority and retry SSH.
options.feedback: Layer 2 root selection does not affect the SSH key algorithm.

options.text: Increase the admin profile privilege level before testing the key.
options.feedback: The access profile is evaluated after authentication, not before the key is accepted.

options.text: Modify the RADIUS accounting proxy retry interval.
options.feedback: RADIUS accounting is not part of this SSH key exchange.

options.text: Compare the client-offered sk algorithm, registered public key, account, and firmware support.
options.feedback: Algorithm mismatch or wrong registered key is an authentication-stage failure.

questions.prompt: A radio defers to weak neighboring signals too often. Which CCA adjustment is consistent with Fortinet's guidance?

options.text: Use a more-negative threshold so the radio senses weaker signals earlier.
options.feedback: A lower threshold increases sensitivity and generally causes more deferral.

options.text: Set the threshold to zero to force maximum channel occupancy.
options.feedback: Zero means unconfigured; the driver uses its predefined value.

options.text: Use a less-negative, higher CCA threshold to ignore weaker signals more often.
options.feedback: A higher threshold reduces sensitivity and deferrals, increasing spatial reuse but also collision risk.

options.text: Increase the DHCP lease time so the radio transmits sooner.
options.feedback: DHCP lease duration does not change radio carrier-sense behavior.

questions.prompt: A dense auditorium needs more spatial reuse. What trade-off must be monitored after raising CCA?

options.text: Lower throughput is guaranteed, but collisions are eliminated completely.
options.feedback: A higher threshold can increase throughput and does not eliminate collisions.

options.text: Only transmit power changes; collision behavior remains identical.
options.feedback: CCA changes the busy/idle decision, not the transmit-power setting.

options.text: The AP will automatically select a different regulatory channel.
options.feedback: CCA threshold tuning does not select a new channel.

options.text: Throughput may rise, but collisions and hidden-node interference can increase.
options.feedback: Raising the threshold reduces deferrals while increasing the chance of simultaneous transmissions.

questions.prompt: A per-AP override is disabled. Which CCA value should the radio inherit?

options.text: The last value entered on the AP remains active regardless of override state.
options.feedback: The per-AP value is not authoritative while override is disabled.

options.text: The assigned WTP profile's radio-specific CCA threshold should remain authoritative.
options.feedback: With override disabled, the AP follows the profile; the profile must be assigned and applied.

options.text: The FortiGate uses the neighbor AP's threshold from the RF scan.
options.feedback: The feature does not automatically copy a neighbor's threshold.

options.text: The AP always uses the default zero threshold after profile assignment.
options.feedback: Zero means unconfigured; a configured profile value should be applied.

questions.prompt: Which command provides the strongest AP-side proof of the effective radio CCA value?

options.text: Run diagnose wireless-controller wlac -c wtp only on the FortiGate.
options.feedback: The controller view is useful, but the AP-side output verifies the effective radio configuration.

options.text: Check only the SSID security profile and WPA authentication counters.
options.feedback: Those settings do not show the radio's CCA threshold.

options.text: Run cw_diag -c radio-cfg on the FortiAP and inspect the radio configuration.
options.feedback: The AP-side radio output shows the value actually applied, including any per-AP override.

options.text: Inspect the DHCP server lease table for the AP management address.
options.feedback: The lease table does not show radio carrier-sense configuration.

questions.prompt: A profiling rule returns Fail. What should the Device Profiler do next?

options.text: Continue evaluation with the next enabled rule in rank order.
options.feedback: Fail means the current rule did not match; it is not a stop condition.

options.text: Stop the entire rule chain and leave the host unclassified.
options.feedback: That is the documented behavior for Cannot Evaluate, not Fail.

options.text: Register the host automatically in Inventory regardless of rule settings.
options.feedback: Registration placement is defined by the matching rule, not by every failure.

options.text: Reboot the switch port and delete the host record immediately.
options.feedback: A rule mismatch does not require port bounce or record deletion.

questions.prompt: The first rule reports Cannot Evaluate because its IP data is stale. Why can a lower rule never match?

options.text: Fail and Cannot Evaluate both continue to the next rule automatically.
options.feedback: Only Fail continues; Cannot Evaluate stops evaluation.

options.text: Cannot Evaluate stops the rule chain when required evidence is unavailable or not current.
options.feedback: Unlike Fail, Cannot Evaluate is a data-availability stop condition.

options.text: The Catch All rule always overrides every earlier evaluation result.
options.feedback: Catch All is last and cannot override a stop caused by missing data.

options.text: The host must be associated with a user before any rule can run.
options.feedback: Unknown rogues are precisely the devices the profiler evaluates.

questions.prompt: A static-IP device never sends a DHCP fingerprint. How should the rule set be improved?

options.text: Place the DHCP fingerprint rule at rank one to force a lease renewal.
options.feedback: A static-IP device may never send DHCP, so the rule can stop useful evaluation.

options.text: Delete the Catch All rule so all devices are evaluated by DHCP.
options.feedback: Catch All is a system rule and DHCP is not universal evidence.

options.text: Disable IP-to-MAC polling because static addresses need no identity mapping.
options.feedback: The profiler may still need current IP/MAC information for other methods.

options.text: Move DHCP-dependent rules after methods that can classify the device without DHCP data.
options.feedback: A missing DHCP fingerprint should not block later rules for static-IP hosts.

questions.prompt: A rule is changed and Run is clicked, but an already registered device keeps its old classification. Why?

options.text: The device must wait for the next DHCP lease before every rule change.
options.feedback: Lease renewal matters for DHCP fingerprint collection, not all already-registered devices.

options.text: Run processes eligible rogues; already categorized devices are not re-evaluated.
options.feedback: The profiler does not re-run modified rules against devices that are no longer rogues.

options.text: The Profiled Devices tab hides all registered devices until a reboot.
options.feedback: Visibility depends on placement and user association, not reboot state.

options.text: The new rule is applied only after FortiNAC restarts its database service.
options.feedback: A restart does not change the documented rogue-only re-evaluation scope.

questions.prompt: A FortiNAC-F discovery job contains several IP ranges. What total address ceiling should be planned?

options.text: Keep each individual range below 65,000, regardless of the combined total.
options.feedback: The combined total is the relevant planning limit.

options.text: Limit the discovery to 4,096 addresses because SNMPv3 uses that many OIDs.
options.feedback: The address limit is not derived from the SNMP OID count.

options.text: There is no range ceiling when CDP recursive discovery is enabled.
options.feedback: CDP expansion does not remove the documented seed-range limit.

options.text: Keep the sum of addresses across all ranges at or below 65,000.
options.feedback: The documented limit applies to the total combined range size, not each range independently.

questions.prompt: The initial SNMP-discovered switch exposes neighbor information. What does enabling CDP discovery add?

options.text: It converts every LLDP neighbor into a DHCP host record automatically.
options.feedback: CDP is a network-device neighbor mechanism, not a general DHCP host-registration path.

options.text: FortiNAC can query advertised CDP neighbors and recursively expand the network-device inventory.
options.feedback: CDP provides neighbor edges that allow additional devices to be discovered beyond the seed ranges.

options.text: It bypasses SNMP credentials and discovers devices from MAC addresses alone.
options.feedback: SNMP is still needed to query discovered devices.

options.text: It merges every interface address into one guaranteed unique device model.
options.feedback: The guide warns that multiple interfaces can create duplicate models.

questions.prompt: One physical switch appears as two network-device models after discovery. What documented behavior could explain it?

options.text: CDP always creates one model for every VLAN on the switch.
options.feedback: The documented duplication warning concerns multiple interfaces and SNMP settings.

options.text: Multiple interfaces with different IP addresses and SNMP settings can create duplicate models.
options.feedback: FortiNAC-F does not automatically consolidate those multi-interface representations in the described case.

options.text: The discovery container has exceeded the 65,000-address range limit.
options.feedback: The range limit can constrain discovery, but it does not explain interface-based duplicates.

options.text: FortiNAC-F converts every SNMPv3 user into a separate network device.
options.feedback: SNMP user identity is not the documented cause of duplicate models.

questions.prompt: Ping to a FortiNAC-OS interface succeeds, but SNMP discovery fails. Which check is most specific?

options.text: Enable HTTPS only and rely on the web interface to answer SNMP probes.
options.feedback: HTTPS access does not enable the SNMP management service.

options.text: Change the discovery container name and increase its polling frequency.
options.feedback: Container naming does not repair SNMP reachability or credentials.

options.text: Verify allowaccess includes snmp and confirm UDP/161 credentials and return-path ACLs.
options.feedback: Ping proves ICMP reachability, not SNMP service enablement or SNMP authentication.

options.text: Replace CDP with DHCP relay because the switch already responds to ping.
options.feedback: DHCP relay is unrelated to SNMP discovery.

questions.prompt: Why would an organization deploy the FortiAuthenticator RADIUS accounting proxy?

options.text: To authenticate every wireless client instead of the upstream RADIUS server.
options.feedback: The accounting proxy processes accounting records after the access decision.

options.text: To replace LDAP with local passwords for all RADIUS users.
options.feedback: LDAP can enrich group attributes; the proxy does not replace the authentication server.

options.text: To transform accounting attributes and replicate records to multiple RSSO destinations.
options.feedback: The proxy solves a one-source-to-many-subscribers problem while applying attribute rules.

options.text: To forward only RADIUS Access-Accept messages to a single switch.
options.feedback: The feature is an accounting fan-out path with configurable destinations.

questions.prompt: Accounting records arrive at FortiAuthenticator but one FortiGate has no RSSO session. What should be compared first?

options.text: Change the upstream Access-Request password on the carrier RADIUS server.
options.feedback: The failure is on one accounting destination, not necessarily authentication.

options.text: Increase the FortiGate policy session timeout before checking accounting packets.
options.feedback: Policy session timeout does not create an RSSO user session.

options.text: Check that destination's address, shared secret, source binding, and applied rule set.
options.feedback: A source can be valid while one downstream destination rejects or misses the transformed record.

options.text: Disable LDAP group lookup on every source and destination.
options.feedback: A single destination failure should be isolated before changing all transformations.

questions.prompt: A proxied accounting packet needs a Fortinet group attribute derived from directory membership. Which component performs that work?

options.text: The source object changes the RADIUS username into a FortiGate VDOM.
options.feedback: Sources identify the upstream server and secret; they do not perform group enrichment.

options.text: A matching rule set can look up LDAP group membership and add the attribute.
options.feedback: The rule set transforms the accounting record using the configured LDAP mapping.

options.text: The destination object creates a new LDAP user for each accounting packet.
options.feedback: Destinations identify receivers; they do not create directory identities.

options.text: The FortiGate firewall policy derives the group before the proxy forwards the packet.
options.feedback: The group attribute must be present in the accounting record for RSSO parsing.

questions.prompt: A user changed directory groups, but proxied RSSO records still show the old group. Which parameter is relevant?

options.text: Review the accounting proxy group-cache lifetime and its last refresh.
options.feedback: A long cache lifetime can retain an older LDAP-derived group mapping.

options.text: Change the FortiGate DHCP lease duration to force a new group lookup.
options.feedback: DHCP lease time does not control FortiAuthenticator's group cache.

options.text: Increase the RADIUS accounting packet identifier to a larger value.
options.feedback: The packet identifier does not refresh cached LDAP membership.

options.text: Disable all proxy retries so the group is always looked up immediately.
options.feedback: Retries govern destination delivery; they do not replace the group-cache lifetime.

questions.prompt: An organization wants FortiPAM membership to follow an LDAP group without importing every user locally. Which group type is appropriate?

options.text: Create a Remote user group and add the LDAP server/group match.
options.feedback: Remote groups project membership from the configured identity source into FortiPAM.

options.text: Create a Local User group and manually copy every LDAP username.
options.feedback: That creates local membership rather than a remote group mapping.

options.text: Add the LDAP server as a secret resource and grant it Owner access.
options.feedback: LDAP is a membership source, not a secret resource.

options.text: Place all LDAP users in everyone and disable remote group matching.
options.feedback: Everyone is a default group, not a scoped mapping of directory membership.

questions.prompt: An LDAP remote group returns too many users. Which control narrows membership to a directory subset?

options.text: Change the FortiPAM session recording retention to reduce the user count.
options.feedback: Recording retention does not affect remote group membership.

options.text: Set the remote group Access option to Customized without defining a filter.
options.feedback: Customized access governs group-object permissions, not LDAP membership selection.

options.text: Increase the RADIUS retry count and leave LDAP matching unchanged.
options.feedback: RADIUS retry settings do not constrain an LDAP remote group.

options.text: Use a directory-specific LDAP filter or select the required remote group.
options.feedback: The filter and group match determine which remote users are projected into the FortiPAM group.

questions.prompt: A user is listed as Owner on a FortiPAM user group. What does that permission mean?

options.text: The user can launch every secret and record every privileged session.
options.feedback: Secret launch rights are governed by separate resource and secret access controls.

options.text: The user can change the LDAP server's global schema and password policy.
options.feedback: FortiPAM group ownership does not grant directory administration.

options.text: The user can create, edit, and delete that user-group object.
options.feedback: Owner/Viewer are group-object management permissions, not automatic vault-wide secret permissions.

options.text: The user can bypass all remote authentication and sign in locally.
options.feedback: Owner is not an authentication method or bypass.

questions.prompt: A user authenticates successfully but is missing from the expected Remote group. What should be checked?

options.text: Change the secret's password rotation schedule before inspecting group membership.
options.feedback: Secret rotation does not control identity group matching.

options.text: Compare the LDAP filter or exact RADIUS/SAML group name with the returned identity attributes.
options.feedback: Authentication success and remote-group membership are separate stages.

options.text: Grant the user Owner on every FortiPAM group and retest.
options.feedback: Owner controls group-object management, not remote membership resolution.

options.text: Disable the identity provider and recreate the FortiPAM appliance.
options.feedback: The targeted issue is group mapping, not appliance initialization.

questions.prompt: Which protocol and default polling interval are documented for FortiEMS discovery?

options.text: Use FORTIEMS_API with the documented five-minute default pull interval.
options.feedback: FortiSIEM polls the EMS Management Server API; it is not an immediate push feed by default.

options.text: Use SNMPv3 traps with a one-minute default polling interval.
options.feedback: The EMS integration uses the FortiEMS API, not SNMP traps.

options.text: Use WMI over TCP/135 with a fifteen-minute default polling interval.
options.feedback: WMI is not the documented FortiEMS integration protocol.

options.text: Use syslog over UDP/514 with a thirty-second default polling interval.
options.feedback: The vulnerability feed is retrieved through the EMS API.

questions.prompt: Vulnerability events are ingested, but the Set tag remediation script fails. Which item is specifically required?

options.text: Verify the FortiEMS serial number and write permissions for the remediation account.
options.feedback: Tag remediation requires the EMS serial number and permissions beyond read-only vulnerability ingestion.

options.text: Increase the CMDB event retention and disable EMS write access.
options.feedback: Retention does not supply the serial number or required write permissions.

options.text: Change the FortiSIEM collector hostname to match the FortiGate serial number.
options.feedback: The remediation script needs the EMS serial number, not a FortiGate identifier.

options.text: Switch the credential protocol from FORTIEMS_API to SNMPv2.
options.feedback: The API integration remains the required management path.

questions.prompt: Which EMS role is sufficient when the requirement is vulnerability ingestion only?

options.text: A read-only EMS role can retrieve vulnerability data without tag-changing permissions.
options.feedback: Write permissions are needed only when FortiSIEM must set or unset endpoint tags.

options.text: A full EMS administrator role is mandatory for every discovery operation.
options.feedback: Fortinet documents read-only access for vulnerability ingestion.

options.text: A FortiGate super_admin role can substitute for an EMS account.
options.feedback: The integration authenticates to EMS, not to the FortiGate.

options.text: A local FortiSIEM analyst role can replace EMS API credentials.
options.feedback: FortiSIEM user roles do not authenticate the EMS API request.

questions.prompt: The EMS tag changes successfully, but a FortiGate still permits the endpoint. What is the missing enforcement check?

options.text: Run the FortiSIEM query again until the endpoint appears in Analytics.
options.feedback: Analytics visibility does not prove the firewall imported or used the tag.

options.text: Increase the FortiEMS polling interval to one day to stabilize the tag.
options.feedback: A slower poll does not create a FortiGate ZTNA rule.

options.text: Confirm the Security Fabric imported the tag and the ZTNA policy references it.
options.feedback: Changing the EMS tag is only the classification step; the enforcement point must consume it in policy.

options.text: Disable endpoint vulnerability polling and clear the FortiGate session table.
options.feedback: The tag import and policy reference must be checked directly.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes FortiSASE DPD modes?

options.text: On-idle probes idle tunnels; on-demand probes when outbound traffic lacks a response; disable only responds.
options.feedback: The modes differ in when the PoP initiates DPD; disable still responds to peer probes.

options.text: On-demand probes continuously; on-idle never sends probes; disable drops all IKE traffic.
options.feedback: Those behaviors reverse the documented DPD semantics.

options.text: On-idle applies only to SSL tunnels; on-demand applies only to DNS requests.
options.feedback: DPD is an IPsec IKE liveness mechanism.

options.text: Disable actively probes every minute, while on-idle disables peer responses.
options.feedback: Disable suppresses active generation but still responds to incoming DPD.

questions.prompt: When does on-demand DPD send a probe according to the feature description?

options.text: At fixed intervals whenever the tunnel has no user traffic.
options.feedback: That describes idle probing, not the on-demand trigger.

options.text: When outbound messages have been sent but no inbound messages arrive during the retry interval.
options.feedback: On-demand ties liveness probing to pending outbound traffic with no response.

options.text: Only after three successful DNS lookups from the endpoint.
options.feedback: DNS success is not the DPD trigger.

options.text: Immediately after every endpoint profile is downloaded.
options.feedback: Profile download does not itself require an IKE DPD probe.

questions.prompt: What is the documented default Security PoP DPD retry window?

options.text: A 60-second retry interval with three missed attempts before the peer is dropped.
options.feedback: The default combines the interval and retry count; together they define the liveness window.

options.text: A 10-second interval with one missed attempt before the peer is dropped.
options.feedback: Those are not the documented defaults.

options.text: A 30-second interval with five missed attempts before the peer is dropped.
options.feedback: The documented default is 60 seconds and three misses.

options.text: A 120-second interval with two missed attempts before the peer is dropped.

questions.prompt: Why should a FortiSASE DPD change be scheduled in a maintenance window?

options.text: The change permanently deletes all endpoint certificates from FortiClient.
options.feedback: The documented impact is a temporary tunnel disconnect, not certificate deletion.

options.text: The change restarts every FortiGate in the Security Fabric.
options.feedback: The change applies to FortiSASE IPsec agent tunnel settings.

options.text: The change forces all users to re-enroll their identity provider accounts.
options.feedback: DPD changes liveness behavior, not user identity enrollment.

options.text: Currently connected endpoints can be disconnected for a few minutes while the change applies.
options.feedback: Fortinet explicitly warns that the DPD change can interrupt connected endpoints.

questions.prompt: A service rule has two SLA-qualified members. What does the tie-break setting do?

options.text: It measures latency and loss for every member from scratch.
options.feedback: Health-check/SLA logic performs the measurement; tie-break selects among qualified candidates.

options.text: It overrides firewall policy and selects a VDOM before routing.
options.feedback: The setting is an SD-WAN member-selection method.

options.text: It creates a new static route for each destination prefix automatically.
options.feedback: Tie-break uses existing routing information; it does not create routes.

options.text: It selects among members that already passed the service's SLA qualification.
options.feedback: SLA qualification creates the candidate set; tie-break chooses among eligible members.

questions.prompt: What is the defining behavior of fib-best-match for service-SLA tie-break?

options.text: Choose the member listed first in the service configuration every time.
options.feedback: That is cfg-order, not fib-best-match.

options.text: Choose the member with the lowest measured latency regardless of route.
options.feedback: That is not the FIB longest-prefix method.

options.text: Choose the member that received the most packets in the previous interval.
options.feedback: Traffic volume is not the fib-best-match criterion.

options.text: Choose the SLA-qualified member whose route has the longest prefix match in the FIB.
options.feedback: The native forwarding table's most-specific route influences selection among healthy members.

questions.prompt: A service rule should inherit the zone's configured SLA tie-break method. Which service setting expresses that intent?

options.text: Set the service rule tie-break to cfg-order even when the zone uses FIB matching.
options.feedback: That explicitly selects a different method rather than inheriting the zone setting.

options.text: Set the SLA target to zone and remove all eligible members.
options.feedback: SLA targets and tie-break selection are separate settings.

options.text: Set the firewall policy route to zone and disable SD-WAN health checks.
options.feedback: Policy routing does not configure the SD-WAN tie-break.

options.text: Set the service rule tie-break to zone so it uses the zone-level value.
options.feedback: The service rule can inherit the zone's service-sla-tie-break behavior.

questions.prompt: Which description correctly distinguishes the four documented tie-break methods?

options.text: cfg-order uses latency; fib-best-match uses packet count; priority uses ingress; input-device uses route prefix.
options.feedback: The criteria are assigned to the wrong methods.

options.text: cfg-order uses ingress; fib-best-match uses configured order; priority uses DNS; input-device uses loss.
options.feedback: These descriptions do not match the CLI reference.

options.text: cfg-order follows configured order; fib-best-match uses FIB prefix; priority uses cost factor; input-device matches ingress.
options.feedback: Each method uses a different deterministic criterion after SLA qualification.

options.text: All four methods choose the first SLA-qualified member and differ only in logging.
options.feedback: The methods make distinct member-selection decisions.

questions.prompt: A recent SD-WAN case shows implicit-rule spillover after an ingress threshold. Why should it not be diagnosed as fib-best-match failure immediately?

options.text: Implicit-rule threshold/session timing is separate from the zone SLA tie-break applied after member qualification.
options.feedback: The two mechanisms operate at different decision stages and need separate evidence.

options.text: Both features use the same FIB longest-prefix lookup, so the symptoms are interchangeable.
options.feedback: Implicit-rule spillover is not the zone's service-SLA tie-break algorithm.

options.text: Implicit rules are controlled by FortiAuthenticator accounting proxy settings.
options.feedback: The feature belongs to SD-WAN service processing, not RADIUS accounting.

options.text: A failed implicit rule always proves that all SLA members are down.
options.feedback: Threshold/session behavior does not prove the health-check state.

questions.prompt: FortiSIEM sets an EMS endpoint tag, but ZTNA access remains unchanged. Which evidence chain is required?

options.text: Verify only that the FortiSIEM incident closed successfully.
options.feedback: Incident closure does not prove tag propagation or firewall policy enforcement.

options.text: Verify EMS tag, Security Fabric import, and the FortiGate ZTNA policy match in sequence.
options.feedback: Each stage proves classification, propagation, and enforcement respectively.

options.text: Verify only that the EMS API returned HTTP 200 during discovery.
options.feedback: API reachability does not prove the tag changed or was imported.

options.text: Verify only that the endpoint has a CMDB record in FortiSIEM.
options.feedback: CMDB presence does not prove the tag or ZTNA rule is active.
